AR.name: Biznaga
AR.citation: SINAVIMO (Sistema Nacional Argentino de Vigilancia y Monitoreo de Plagas), official government pest/weed database, listing it as present in the country affecting maize and alfalfa crops; Flora Bonaerense documents genuine medicinal use in Buenos Aires province for chronic asthma, psoriasis, hypertension and vitiligo, alongside its listed toxicity risks

CL.name: Biznaga
CL.citation: Khalil et al. (2020), peer-reviewed pharmacognosy review (Molecules journal, PMC7024292), confirming genuine naturalized distribution in Chile alongside Argentina and Mexico

DE.name: Knorpelmohre
DE.citation: A.Vogel Plant Encyclopaedia; named for its umbel resemblance to Daucus carota (carrot), with the German name literally meaning 'gristle/knobbed carrot'. Genuine European homeopathic/phytotherapy use documented since Dioscorides

EG.name: Khella Baladi
EG.citation: Ask-Ayurveda; A.Vogel Plant Encyclopaedia. Used therapeutically by ancient Egyptians, documented in the Ebers Papyrus for kidney stones and bilharzia-related urinary calculi; dried umbels still sold in Middle Eastern markets today, used as toothpicks

ES.name: Viznaga
ES.citation: Fitoterapia.net vademecum; Hierbitas.com. The Iberian source of the 'biznaga/viznaga' naming tradition later carried to Latin America. Also used to make the traditional floral ornament 'biznagas malaguenas' from the dried plant skeleton in Malaga, Spain

GB.name: Khella
GB.citation: Drugs.com clinical monograph; the source of khellin, from which the modern asthma drug sodium cromoglycate was derived in 1967. Also documented as bishop's weed (not to be confused with Ajwain, a different plant) and toothpick weed

MA.name: Bachnikha
MA.citation: Phytochemistry and medicinal properties of Ammi visnaga (Apiaceae), peer-reviewed review. Morocco is one of the plant's core cultivation regions alongside Egypt and Tunisia

MX.name: Biznaga
MX.citation: Confirmed naturalized in Mexico (Khalil et al. 2020, PMC7024292; tusplantasmedicinales.com). IMPORTANT CROSS-SPECIES CAUTION: in Mexico 'biznaga' is also, and more commonly, the name for several native barrel cacti (e.g. Echinocactus platyacanthus, used to make the candy acitron) - an entirely unrelated plant family. Sources explicitly warn not to confuse 'las biznagas mexicanas' (the native cacti) with this species

PT.name: Bisnaga-das-searas
PT.citation: EcuRed; Fitoterapia.net vademecum. Also documented as paliteira. The Iberian Portuguese source of naming later relevant to Brazilian Portuguese usage

US.name: Khella
US.citation: Drugs.com clinical monograph; naturalized to parts of the southeastern United States. SAFETY: khellin can cause photosensitivity and liver enzyme changes at high doses
